notes.beat: Even in Babylon God gives Daniel the seventy-weeks timetable dating Messiah — the Advent was published, and a remnant watched.
notes.oldNote: Because even in Babylon, in the palace of the power that burned His house, He was showing His servant Daniel the timetable of hope: 'Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people… unto the Messiah the Prince' (Daniel 9:24-25) — a prophecy so precise it dated the Messiah's arrival, His ministry, and His death, centuries in advance. Anyone who searched could know the time. And some did: a quiet remnant waited — Simeon watching, Anna praying in the temple courts — and wise men far in the east read heaven's clock and saddled their camels. Mark this: the Advent was never meant to be a surprise. It was published.
notes.newNote:
Picture the ruin behind this moment. The temple is ash, the city broken, the people marched off in chains to Babylon — the very power that burned God's house. And there, inside the palace of the empire that had swallowed His people, God is not silent. He is bending over an exile named Daniel, handing him a clock.

Not comfort in the abstract — a date. "Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people... unto the Messiah the Prince" (Daniel 9:24-25). A prophecy so exact it fixed the year the Deliverer would come, the year He would begin His ministry, the year He would die — centuries before any of it happened. Heaven had set the hour in council, and now it was written down where anyone who searched could find it. God's promises, as the old account puts it, know no haste and no delay; when the great clock of time pointed to that hour, He would come.

And some were watching the clock. Down the centuries a quiet remnant kept the faith alive — steadfast souls still looking for the hope of the promise: old Simeon lingering in the temple, Anna praying through the night, waiting. And far to the east, wise men read the same heaven-sent signs, saddled their camels, and at every stop on the long road pulled out the ancient scrolls and searched the prophecies again.

So mark this — the one thing your listener should carry out the door: the Advent was never meant to catch the world by surprise. It was announced. It was dated. It was published. God told us He was coming, and then He came.

notes.beat: The serpent's oldest move — 'Yea, hath God said?' — buries the plain Word under tradition before the first advent.
notes.oldNote: But watch the counter-move — it is the oldest one in the Book. The serpent's first recorded words were a question about words: 'Yea, hath God said?' (Genesis 3:1). In the centuries before the first advent he asked it again, through gentler voices: surely the prophecy is figurative; surely the tradition of the elders knows best; surely the scholars will tell you what it really means. Layer by layer — commentary, tradition, politics — the plain Word was buried alive: 'making the word of God of none effect through your tradition' (Mark 7:13). The scrolls never left the lecterns. The understanding left the scrolls. A nation can hold the Book in both hands and lose it completely.
notes.newNote:
But watch the counter-move — it is the oldest one in the Book. The serpent's very first recorded words were a question about words: "Yea, hath God said?" (Genesis 3:1). And in the long centuries before the first advent, he asked it again — not with a hiss, but through gentler, more respectable voices: surely the prophecy is only figurative; surely the tradition of the elders knows best; surely the learned rabbis will tell you what it really means.

So the teachers of Israel stopped sowing the seed of the Word. They dwelt on tradition, on human theories, and — this is the sentence to feel — what men had written about the Word they slowly set in the place of the Word itself. Layer by layer, commentary and custom and politics were stacked on top of Scripture until the plain promise was buried alive: "making the word of God of none effect through your tradition" (Mark 7:13). The scrolls never left the lecterns. The understanding left the scrolls.

Here is the strange part. Outside Israel, Gentiles reading those same prophecies sometimes understood them better than the priests who guarded them — because the bigotry of the teachers had hindered the very light they were meant to carry. A nation can hold the Book in both hands and lose it completely.

That is why the true Interpreter had to come in person — to separate truth from the chaff of man's utterance that had made it of none effect, and to meet every buried promise with two plain words that no tradition could smother: "It is written."

notes.beat: When the clock strikes, the nation is asleep — pagan astronomers find the cradle while Jerusalem's theologians miss their hour.
notes.oldNote: But when the clock struck, the nation was asleep. The very scrolls that dated the Messiah sat in the temple, read aloud every Sabbath by scholars who missed their own hour. Pagan astronomers followed a star across deserts to the cradle — while Jerusalem's theologians, five miles away, had to look the address up for them (Matthew 2:4-6)… and then went back to bed. The darkness was not a lack of light; it was the enemy's oldest craft: a people slowly bewitched by tradition, position and politics until, 'seeing, they see not.' They knew the prophecies by heart. And they did not know 'the time of thy visitation' (Luke 19:44).
notes.newNote:
But when the clock finally struck, the nation was asleep. All heaven was awake — angels had come to Jerusalem itself, to the very priests and scholars who guarded the sacred scrolls, and found them rehearsing prayers they no longer heard. Every morning the temple lamb was slain, every Sabbath the prophecies were read aloud that dated this exact hour — and the men who read them were not preparing to meet anyone. Only a few, somewhere, were still watching for the Unseen.

So the announcement went elsewhere. To poor shepherds on a hillside. And then, from a thousand miles east, pagan stargazers came following a light across the desert, asking, "Where is he that is born King of the Jews?" The rabbis knew the answer cold — Bethlehem, five miles down the road (Matthew 2:4-6). They turned to the scroll, read Micah's prophecy aloud to strangers... and did not walk out the gate to see. The wise men left the holy city less certain than when they arrived, and went on alone. The theologians went back to their duties.

That is the darkness — not an absence of light, but a people so bewitched by tradition, position and politics that "seeing, they see not." They had the address memorized. They simply did not know "the time of their visitation" (Luke 19:44). The tragedy was never that the truth was hidden. It was standing five miles away, and no one bothered to go.

notes.beat: Heaven was never a spectator — in all their affliction He was afflicted; the God of this Book feels the suffering from inside.
notes.oldNote: 'In all their affliction He was afflicted' (Isaiah 63:9). Heaven was never a spectator. Long before Bethlehem, every tear down here was felt up there — the Son at the edge of glory, weeping over a world He would not abandon. And when He finally came down, the shortest verse in the Book records what He carried: 'Jesus wept' (John 11:35). The God of this Book feels the suffering from the inside. Unique among all the answers. Let it breathe.
notes.newNote:
"In all their affliction He was afflicted" (Isaiah 63:9). Heaven was never a spectator. Story of Redemption pulls back the curtain: when man fell, sorrow filled heaven — but it was the Son whose face carried the sympathy and the sorrow. Three times He stepped into the light around the Father, pleading, until He came out having offered His own life. So this rescue was never distant charity. As the writer put it, the pain "did not begin or end" at Bethlehem — every tear down here was already felt up there, long before He came, the Son at the edge of glory weeping over a world He would not abandon.

And when He finally came down, the shortest verse in the Book records what He carried: "Jesus wept" (John 11:35). The cross only made visible, to our dull senses, what had been true from the start — the God of this Book feels the suffering from the inside.

Unique among all the answers. Let it breathe.

notes.beat: The entering began in a manger — Christ took human nature in all its frailties, carrying it through suffering to death.
notes.oldNote: And where did that entering begin? A manger. Jesus took upon Himself human nature in all its frailties. He was hungry, tired, tempted — and He carried that nature through suffering and blood to death, that we might be redeemed.
notes.newNote:
So where did that entering begin? Not in a palace — in a stable, a newborn laid in a feeding-trough for animals. The King of heaven veiled His glory in the body of a helpless baby, and came into the very world Satan claimed as his own. He took up our nature in all its frailty — He grew hungry, grew tired, was tempted at every turn — and He didn't come shielded. He came to fight the battle every one of us fights, at the real risk of losing.

Yet heaven knew what this manger meant. Angels lit up the night over shepherds and sang, because the Son of God had come to a broken world to do one thing: carry that borrowed human nature all the way through suffering, through blood, to death — so that we could be brought home. He was treated as we deserve, that we might be treated as He deserves. That is where our rescue begins — not on a throne, but in a manger.

notes.beat: The wilderness rematch: where the first Adam fell full-fed, the last Adam stands starving, beating the enemy with 'It is written.'
notes.oldNote: And before His public ministry, He walked into a rematch. Eden again — reversed in every detail. The first Adam fell in a garden, full-fed, surrounded by every delight; the last Adam stood in a desert, starving after forty days. And the enemy came with the same three-stranded rope: appetite — 'command that these stones be made bread'; presumption — 'cast thyself down'; and the old original offer — the kingdoms of the world for one act of worship, the same bargain he had been selling to nations for four thousand years. Now watch the Champion's weapon. Not one bolt of Deity. Three times, only this: 'It is written' (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). The Book the serpent had spent forty centuries burying was the sword that beat him — wielded by a man. Where the first Adam fell, the second stood. And He stood using nothing that is not also in your hands.
notes.newNote:
And before He ever preached a sermon, He walked into a rematch — the oldest fight in the world, run again, reversed in every detail. The first Adam fell in a garden: full-fed, surrounded by every delight, the love of God shining out of everything his eye rested on. The last Adam stood in a desert — pale, emaciated, forty days without a bite of food, alone among the wild beasts in a desolate place where everything around Him was repulsive. Just where the ruin began, the rescue had to begin.

And the enemy came in close, because he thought he finally had the advantage. This time God had humbled Himself down into a man — weak, starving, at the very end of His strength. Satan pressed the same three-stranded rope he'd been selling for four thousand years: appetite — "command that these stones be made bread"; presumption — "cast Thyself down"; and the old original bargain — all the kingdoms of the world for one act of worship.

Now watch the Champion's weapon. Not one bolt of Deity. Three times, only this: "It is written" (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). And here's what the enemy was really fighting for: he knew that if this Man went through with the rescue, his own kingdom was finished. So he threw everything he had — and lost to a starving man holding nothing but a Book. Where the first Adam fell, the second stood. And He stood using nothing that isn't also in your hands.

notes.beat: The King enters Jerusalem lowly on a donkey as prophecy said — riding not to a throne but to His judgment, and He weeps over the city.
notes.oldNote: And when He came, He came precisely the way the prophecy said: 'behold, thy King cometh unto thee… lowly, and riding upon an ass' (Zechariah 9:9). The crowds waved palms and shouted Hosanna — expecting Him to mount the throne of David that very week and break the neck of Rome. But He was not riding to a coronation. He was walking to His judgment and His sacrifice. And He knew what their misplaced expectation would become when it curdled — the same voices crying Hosanna on Sunday would cry Crucify by Friday. So as the city came into view, the King on the donkey did what He had done at the balustrade of heaven: 'And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it' (Luke 19:41).
notes.newNote:
And when He finally came, He came exactly the way the prophet had written five hundred years before: "behold, thy King cometh unto thee... lowly, and riding upon an ass" (Zechariah 9:9). This was the mount kings of Israel rode to their coronation, and the crowd knew it. They tore branches from the palms, threw their own coats down as a carpet in the dust, and the shout went up — Hosanna! In their minds they could already see it: the Roman legions driven out, David's throne restored, Israel free again by the end of the week. The whole city emptied toward Him; the priests blew the trumpet for evening prayer and no one came. "The world is gone after Him," they said in alarm.

But the King on the donkey was not riding to a crown. He knew — the way you know a thing that breaks your heart — that this same road ran straight to a cross, and that the voices crying Hosanna on Sunday would be the voices crying Crucify by Friday.

So at the crest of the hill, with Jerusalem spread out golden below Him in the setting sun, He stopped. And He wept. Not for Himself — Gethsemane and Calvary were right there in front of Him, and He never flinched from them. He wept for the city. He saw what she was, and what she might have been if only she had known Him. He had come to save her. How could He give her up? "And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it" (Luke 19:41).

notes.beat: The accuser's sharpest charge: if the law is just the lawbreaker cannot be pardoned — justice and mercy cannot coexist.
notes.oldNote: The accuser's sharpest charge: if the law is just, the lawbreaker cannot be pardoned; justice and mercy cannot coexist. Every human court faces this. The cross takes both horns.
notes.newNote:
Here is the accuser's sharpest charge, and he has pressed it from the opening of the great war. Listen to him: God's law is just — good — but if it is truly just, then a lawbreaker simply cannot be pardoned. Every sin must meet its punishment. So either God upholds the law and the sinner is lost, or He forgives the sinner and His own justice becomes a lie. Justice and mercy, the accuser insists, stand apart — separated by a gulf no one can cross.

And notice: every human court still faces exactly this. Let the guilty go and you mock the law; punish them and there is no mercy. We have never solved it.

Then look at the cross. God does not soften the law by a single word — not a jot, not a tittle. Instead He steps into the sinner's place Himself. The One hanging there is "counted a transgressor," the guilt of every one of us pressed upon His heart; He takes the full judicial weight of a broken law so that we can go free. The law is satisfied — and the sinner is pardoned. The cross does not choose between the two horns. It takes both at once. Here mercy and truth finally meet; justice and mercy embrace.

notes.beat: At the cross God does not change the rules — He absorbs the penalty Himself; justice satisfied and mercy extended.
notes.oldNote: God did not change the rules to excuse us — He absorbed the penalty Himself (2 Corinthians 5:19). Justice satisfied AND mercy extended. The Lawgiver pays the law's own price. Reverent; let the weight of it land.
notes.newNote:
Picture the charge Satan had pressed since the war in heaven: that God's law could never be obeyed, and that if it were broken, mercy and justice could not both stand — pardon the sinner and God is no longer just; punish him and there is no mercy. Heaven itself knew the law could not be softened or set aside to rescue us. So God did the unthinkable. He did not change the rules to excuse us — the Lawgiver stepped down and paid the law's own price Himself. On that cross the iniquity of every one of us was laid on His Son; He was counted a transgressor, bore the full weight of the penalty as our substitute, and drank the cup to its bitter dregs (2 Corinthians 5:19).

And here justice and mercy meet. The penalty is paid in full — justice satisfied — and the sinner walks free — mercy extended. Neither is bent; both are honored, in one act of self-emptying love.

Then, in a voice that seemed to ring through all creation, He cried, "It is finished." Reverent here. Slow down. Let the weight of it land — the Judge took the sentence so that we would never have to.

notes.beat: The cross publicly exposes the powers of darkness — by killing the Author of life, the accuser's own cause is condemned before the universe.
notes.oldNote: At the cross the powers of darkness were publicly exposed in what they did to the only innocent man who ever lived (Colossians 2:15 — 'made a shew of them openly'). The accuser's own cause condemned him: the government he promised was better ended by killing the Author of life. Whatever sympathy his case still had died at the cross, in full view of the watching universe. (Revelation 12:10-11 names him 'the accuser' cast down by 'the blood of the Lamb' — same scene, same verdict.)
notes.newNote:
Watch what the cross does to the darkness itself. Every power that had been hiding behind respectable faces — the courts, the crowd, the accuser working through them all — is dragged into the light by the one thing it does here: it kills the only innocent man who ever lived, the very Author of life. Paul says God stripped those powers bare at the cross and "made a shew of them openly" (Colossians 2:15). For ages the accuser had whispered that God's way was unfair and his own way would be better — and the watching universe had never fully seen through it. Now they see. By shedding the blood of the Son of God, the accuser reveals himself as a murderer, and whatever sympathy his cause still held anywhere in creation dies with the innocent. The government he promised would be kinder ends by nailing goodness itself to a beam.

And at the instant Jesus bows His head — "It is finished" — the verdict lands. Heaven had said it plainly: "the accuser of our brethren is cast down" (Revelation 12:10). Same scene, same sentence. He is defeated, and he knows his kingdom is lost.
